questions.q: At a channel flip rate of p = 0.08, the verified computation gives a success probability of 0.981824 for the 3-bit repetition code. What does the remaining 0.018176 represent?
options: The probability that 2 or 3 of the 3 bits flip, causing majority vote to decode incorrectly
The probability that exactly 0 bits flip
The probability that the channel has no noise at all
The probability that the code is not usable at this flip rate
questions.explain: 1 minus the success probability is exactly the probability of the majority-failure cases: 2 or 3 of the 3 bits flipping.

questions.q: What does a code's 'minimum distance' measure?
options: The smallest number of bit positions in which any two distinct valid codewords differ
The number of bits used to encode the message
The average time it takes to decode a codeword
The number of codewords that exist in the code
questions.explain: Minimum distance is a property of the codeword set itself -- the smallest Hamming distance between any two distinct codewords.

questions.q: Why does the 3-bit repetition code (minimum distance 3) correct exactly 1 error, no more?
options: By the rule t = floor((d-1)/2), distance 3 gives floor(2/2) = 1 correctable error
Because 3-bit codes can never correct any errors at all
Because the code's minimum distance is actually 1, not 3
Because majority vote always fails on exactly 2 errors regardless of code length
questions.explain: Plugging d=3 into t = floor((d-1)/2) gives exactly 1, matching the code's actual observed behavior of correcting 1 flip and failing at 2 or more.

questions.q: The 5-bit repetition code has minimum distance 5. How many errors can it correct, using the d >= 2t+1 rule?
options: 2 errors, since floor((5-1)/2) = 2
5 errors, one for each bit
1 error, same as the 3-bit code
0 errors -- 5-bit codes can only detect, not correct
questions.explain: floor((d-1)/2) with d=5 gives floor(4/2) = 2, matching the earlier success-probability table where the 5-bit code's majority vote survives up to 2 simultaneous flips.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this distance-to-correction relationship (d >= 2t+1) matters beyond classical repetition codes?
options: The same relationship applies unchanged to quantum codes -- e.g. the Steane [[7,1,3]] code corrects exactly 1 error because its minimum distance is 3
It only applies to codes with an odd number of bits
It has no further relevance once quantum codes are introduced
Quantum codes use a completely different, unrelated distance formula
questions.explain: The [[7,1,3]] notation for the Steane code (built in chapter 4) names its distance (3) directly, and that distance determines its correction power via the exact same rule used here for classical repetition codes.
